powers.txt: Their powers Comic book · unbreakable footing · own recoil · safe passenger · air 50% absorbed · never knocked back All of these are their absorption at work, used on purpose. Each switch suspends one piece of real physics, on purpose. Everything else stays real. Comic-book physics is their default: Unbreakable footing, They take their own recoil, Things keep their form, Safe passenger and Air resistance absorbed are on unless you turn them off (they choose when not to use them), and so is Never knocked back, one switch each. Bolted and the other switches are off by default. (The Collide tab’s two thought experiments, Truly immovable and Light speed, stay on that tab: they are about the test, not their powers.) Muscle physics Comic book Real muscle Each move uses a fixed share of his strength at any speed, set to match real athletes at record-human strength. Above that, speed keeps growing with the square root of strength. Holding their ground Bolted to the planet Rex Ollie On, a push along the ground can’t slide his planted feet: it goes into the planet instead. He still walks, runs and jumps. What else it changes depends on the move, and each tab says so: weak ground can still give way under him, and in some two-player tests the ground around his feet can tear out or a very fast hit is over before the bolts can help (Unbreakable footing rules out both). Off, he is just standing, and friction holds him. One each, so a contest can bolt one side and not the other. For their own throws, punches, stomps, pulls, shoves and catches, They take their own recoil keeps them planted too, but it sends the push back to their source, the endless ocean, and with both on that is where it goes. (For a pull it takes only the rope’s pull back: his own steps are the move, so they still push on the ground.) Never knocked back Rex Ollie On, a hit from outside a contest doesn’t move him: its momentum goes to their source, the endless ocean, even if he is bolted, and the energy it frees where he stands is taken back unless he means it (canon). Off, it moves him as real physics says. In their contests, every two-player test here, they let force move: the other’s push on him is real, and only his own push back is taken (They take their own recoil). A catch is his own push too, so that power takes it back. So this switch acts in one case only: a throw that reaches the catcher as a fireball or plasma in the game of catch (Things keep their form off, some of the air’s drag left), which hits him rather than being caught. Unbreakable footing: the ground under them never breaks: no craters, cracked slabs, sinking or punching through. They take back the energy that would break it. Each push that reaches the ground still goes in, so the ground shakes as it would. Where the ground couldn’t bear a push (a big jump, a heavy lift, standing at huge density), their power holds it. Footprints in soil stay. The “Break the ground” effort turns it off for that move. They take their own recoil: the push back from their own throws, punches, stomps, pulls and shoves, and from stopping what they catch, goes into their source, the endless ocean, not into the planet. So their own moves and catches don’t shove them back, launch them or carry them off, and none of that push back reaches the ground, so it doesn’t shake the ground. The endless ocean takes the whole push back of the move, the other way: the momentum of what they set moving or stop, plus whatever resists it while they push (a pulled load’s rolling or sliding, a shoved partner’s feet). The weight of what they hold up while they push stays on their feet, as on the Lift tab. A punch into air leaves none: when the arm stops, the fist’s momentum comes back. A jump, a sprint start or his steps as he pulls a load are the move itself, not recoil, so they still push on the ground. An incoming hit, such as a throw that reaches the catcher as plasma, isn’t their own push back, so this power doesn’t stop it (Never knocked back does, above). In their contests, every two-player test here, force moves: the other’s push on him is real, and only his own push back goes to the endless ocean. What holds him against the other’s push is his footing, or Bolted. Material limit suspended Things keep their form: what they hold or throw can’t be broken by them or the air: not by their grip, the launch, its own weight, the air’s push or heating in flight. Hitting anything else is real physics (its landing, a miss). People they throw or catch Safe passenger: someone they throw or catch feels only a manageable push, spread through their whole body, at the launch, in the air and when they land, so they come down unharmed. The landing’s push still reaches the ground, so it shakes the ground as a real landing does; its energy, the harm a fall would do, is taken back. It doesn’t cover heating in a very fast flight (Things keep their form does). Only a person is a passenger: Ollie is as tough as Rex. The rest is real: it slows the throw, and the air takes it as a boom, a blast and heat. Their own bodies always meet real air. Silent strike: no blast and no sonic boom from a punch or a clap. Soft landing: no crater or quake when he lands: the impact’s energy is taken back. The ground still takes the same push as his legs stop him, so it can still give way or shake. Absorbed energy goes to Endless ocean (canon) Gradual growth Instant growth Runaway growth Applies to the energy Silent strike and Soft landing take back, the energy Unbreakable footing takes back from the ground, and the Weight tab’s what-if. (Air resistance absorbed cancels drag: what the air would have taken goes to the endless ocean, and the thrown thing keeps its speed, so nothing grows from it.) Endless ocean: it returns to the store they draw on, and nothing changes. Gradual: it becomes mass over a time you set. Instant: all at once. Runaway: instant, and the growth’s own side effects are taken back too. powers.txt: Their powers Comic book · unbreakable footing · own recoil · safe passenger · air 50% absorbed · never knocked back: Ollie All of these are their absorption at work, used on purpose. Each switch suspends one piece of real physics, on purpose. Everything else stays real. Comic-book physics is their default: Unbreakable footing, They take their own recoil, Things keep their form, Safe passenger and Air resistance absorbed are on unless you turn them off (they choose when not to use them), and so is Never knocked back, one switch each. Bolted and the other switches are off by default. (The Collide tab’s two thought experiments, Truly immovable and Light speed, stay on that tab: they are about the test, not their powers.) Muscle physics Comic book Real muscle Each move uses a fixed share of his strength at any speed, set to match real athletes at record-human strength. Above that, speed keeps growing with the square root of strength. Holding their ground Bolted to the planet Rex Ollie On, a push along the ground can’t slide his planted feet: it goes into the planet instead. He still walks, runs and jumps. What else it changes depends on the move, and each tab says so: weak ground can still give way under him, and in some two-player tests the ground around his feet can tear out or a very fast hit is over before the bolts can help (Unbreakable footing rules out both). Off, he is just standing, and friction holds him. One each, so a contest can bolt one side and not the other. For their own throws, punches, stomps, pulls, shoves and catches, They take their own recoil keeps them planted too, but it sends the push back to their source, the endless ocean, and with both on that is where it goes. (For a pull it takes only the rope’s pull back: his own steps are the move, so they still push on the ground.) Never knocked back Rex Ollie On, a hit from outside a contest doesn’t move him: its momentum goes to their source, the endless ocean, even if he is bolted, and the energy it frees where he stands is taken back unless he means it (canon). Off, it moves him as real physics says. In their contests, every two-player test here, they let force move: the other’s push on him is real, and only his own push back is taken (They take their own recoil). A catch is his own push too, so that power takes it back. So this switch acts in one case only: a throw that reaches the catcher as a fireball or plasma in the game of catch (Things keep their form off, some of the air’s drag left), which hits him rather than being caught. Unbreakable footing: the ground under them never breaks: no craters, cracked slabs, sinking or punching through. They take back the energy that would break it. Each push that reaches the ground still goes in, so the ground shakes as it would. Where the ground couldn’t bear a push (a big jump, a heavy lift, standing at huge density), their power holds it. Footprints in soil stay. The “Break the ground” effort turns it off for that move. They take their own recoil: the push back from their own throws, punches, stomps, pulls and shoves, and from stopping what they catch, goes into their source, the endless ocean, not into the planet. So their own moves and catches don’t shove them back, launch them or carry them off, and none of that push back reaches the ground, so it doesn’t shake the ground. The endless ocean takes the whole push back of the move, the other way: the momentum of what they set moving or stop, plus whatever resists it while they push (a pulled load’s rolling or sliding, a shoved partner’s feet). The weight of what they hold up while they push stays on their feet, as on the Lift tab. A punch into air leaves none: when the arm stops, the fist’s momentum comes back. A jump, a sprint start or his steps as he pulls a load are the move itself, not recoil, so they still push on the ground. An incoming hit, such as a throw that reaches the catcher as plasma, isn’t their own push back, so this power doesn’t stop it (Never knocked back does, above). In their contests, every two-player test here, force moves: the other’s push on him is real, and only his own push back goes to the endless ocean. What holds him against the other’s push is his footing, or Bolted. Material limit suspended Things keep their form: what they hold or throw can’t be broken by them or the air: not by their grip, the launch, its own weight, the air’s push or heating in flight. Hitting anything else is real physics (its landing, a miss). People they throw or catch Safe passenger: someone they throw or catch feels only a manageable push, spread through their whole body, at the launch, in the air and when they land, so they come down unharmed. The landing’s push still reaches the ground, so it shakes the ground as a real landing does; its energy, the harm a fall would do, is taken back. It doesn’t cover heating in a very fast flight (Things keep their form does). Only a person is a passenger: Ollie is as tough as Rex. Absorbed (energy goes back into them) Air resistance absorbed 50%the air takes 50% of the drag: a fast throw slows less, but still booms and makes a smaller blast 0% (real air)100% (drag-free) The share of the air’s drag on what they throw that they cancel: the push and energy the air would have exchanged go to the endless ocean (canon), so the thing keeps its speed. The rest is real: it slows the throw, and the air takes it as a boom, a blast and heat. Their own bodies always meet real air. Silent strike: no blast and no sonic boom from a punch or a clap. Soft landing: no crater or quake when he lands: the impact’s energy is taken back. The ground still takes the same push as his legs stop him, so it can still give way or shake. Absorbed energy goes to Endless ocean (canon) Gradual growth Instant growth Runaway growth Applies to the energy Silent strike and Soft landing take back, the energy Unbreakable footing takes back from the ground, and the Weight tab’s what-if. (Air resistance absorbed cancels drag: what the air would have taken goes to the endless ocean, and the thrown thing keeps its speed, so nothing grows from it.) Endless ocean: it returns to the store they draw on, and nothing changes. Gradual: it becomes mass over a time you set. Instant: all at once. Runaway: instant, and the growth’s own side effects are taken back too. math: Aim: the gentlest throw is the angle needing the least launch speed, each speed solved so the arc comes down at Ollie’s hand height (2.74 m) where his hands meet it, 1.82 m in front of his centre. Same air and round-Earth model as Throw. Fastball: his full-strength speed at each angle; the flattest angle whose path passes Ollie’s hands. Catch: first contact with his hands (m_h = 132 kg): v₁ = v m/(m + m_h); energy lost ½ m m_h v²/(m + m_h), over a 3 cm–7.6 cm squash (1–2.5% of his height, an estimate). Then his feet hold (They take their own recoil: he is planted): F = (m + m_h) v₁²/(2d) + m g sin(angle), up to the most his arms can push; if that isn’t enough, it reaches his chest at v² = v₁² − 2d(F − m g sin(angle))/(m + m_h). d = 0.3 × his height = 91 cm. First contact lasts about 2 × squash / v. At the arm force F the stroke takes t = (v₁ − v)/a (v = 0 where his arms stop it), a = (F − m g sin(angle))/(m + m_h); at the least force that works, t = 2d/v₁. The round trip counts that stroke only when it is forced (his arms can’t stop it, or need at least half his strength); otherwise he can take as long as he likes. Nose heating (Sutton–Graves): q = 1.74 × 10⁻⁴ √(ρ/rₙ) v³ W/m², added up along the path; radiation ceiling σ(T⁴ − T₀⁴) below 30 km only (higher up radiation is left out, so the top end runs low on high flights); share ≈ heat × frontal area / (mass × heat to char 1 kg).

fb-before.verdict: At 96.4% of light speed the baseball turns into a fireball within about 47.1 m of Rex’s hand, before it reaches Ollie. The fireball keeps rushing toward him, and what hits him 10 km away is a blast carrying up to 36.1 PJ, the heat made in the air (its motion as it reaches him is taken back: below). Never knocked back: it doesn’t move Ollie. Its momentum (160 million kg·m/s) goes to the endless ocean, and stopping it frees 36.3 PJ where he stands.
